utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, and Vladimir Santic, alias Vlado.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Moskowitz, you may, of course, resume your examination-in-chief. May I ask you and the witness to be so kind as to speak slowly, and particularly the witness, after you put your question, should wait for half a minute, so that the interpreters can translate, interpret everything into French and Serbo-Croatian. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Watters, we left off yesterday, I believe, with your having described the situation as it occurred to you the morning of April 16th, 1993, in the Vitez headquarters, where you were receiving reports of firing and fighting. Could you tell us again the nature of those reports that you were receiving that morning as you were in the ops room of your headquarters in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The initial reports came from static positions that we had and included reports or a report from the Dutch transport squadron near Santici and our own logistic base outside Vitez. The reports centred on widespread fighting or shooting, a great deal of houses on fire up and down the Lasva Valley, and what was most puzzling of all were reports of large mortar and artillery exchanges or shootings; between 200 and 300 artillery and mortar rounds had landed that morning in the area of Vitez and its environs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, as you were receiving those reports, did you have a clear sense of what, in fact, was going on in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we didn't, sir. We couldn't work out what on earth was happening initially in the early hours of the 16th. The scale of the fighting had taken us totally by surprise. As I explained, our focus at that time was really in Tuzla and the fighting in eastern Bosnia between the Serbs and the BiH, and the evacuation of injured and civilians from Srbrenica which our "C" company was doing at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then take steps to determine what, in fact, was going on, and I know yesterday you talked about sending out reconnaissance missions, but now I am speaking about steps that you personally took so that you could assure yourself as to what was happening in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At approximately 8.00 or 8.30, I decided to take a patrol out myself to get a feel for what the substance was that our reconnaissance patrols had been reporting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me stop you there for a moment. Would that have been unusual for you to actually leave the operations room while your superior commander was not in the operations room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be unusual, sir, but as the commanding officer was in Zenica, I was the de facto commanding officer and felt that I had to go and get a feel on the ground for what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I took a Warrior patrol, Warrior being our armoured fighting vehicle, I took a patrol of, I think, two or four Warriors, and went through Vitez and down the valley, I think as far as the turning up to Jelinak or the junction with Busovaca, I can't exactly remember how far away, but I went a way down the valley, and then returned via Vitez where we contacted the brigade commander for the HVO forces in Vitez and the town commander for the BiH forces in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as you travelled through the town of Vitez, taking that area first, could you describe what you saw as you went down the road through Vitez, and perhaps it might be illustrative of your testimony if you could, with the permission of the Court, go to Exhibit 1, which is the big area map of the Lasva River Valley and describe what you saw by showing us the route you took along the Lasva Valley, if you would, with the permission of the Court? Yes, you may go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I came out of our base at Bila school and travelled up the road towards Vitez, took the right fork here to go into Vitez town, and when I got to -- I went past our own base here, our logistic base, drove into the town, and from about this point here, I could see great palls of smoke coming from the centre of the town, but there were no signs of fighting in the outskirts here. As I drove through the outskirts, we then came into the rear of the Muslim area of Vitez, Stari Vitez, and there was considerable fighting and sniping against our own vehicles as we moved across the interface between the Croat part of the town and the Muslim part of the town. The contrast on crossing the line of battle here was quite stark in that the centre of Vitez, Stari Vitez, looked like a battle ground. There were rocket launcher hits on the houses, there were an awful lot of bullet strikes on the fronts of the houses, there were dead bodies in the streets and dead bodies hanging out of windows, certainly one is very vivid to me, and there weren't massive amounts of bodies, probably about seven, ten bodies within that area of the street. I didn't turn left or right into the streets because we were closed down, and our vision, when we have the components on our vehicles closed, is quite restricted and we were frightened that we would cause great damage to the buildings. So we moved through the town and across a very obvious interface just below the Hotel Vitez or another line of battle, where we moved through the Muslim quarter and into the second part of the -- the Croat part of the town, and again, the contrast was stark in that there were no scenes of battle, there was no destruction. In fact, it was just quite bizarre. And then we moved through Vitez, and the top part of Vitez here, although deserted, looked as it always had. I mean, there had been no fighting there. And then I moved on round over the bridge down to the junction and then moved up through Dubravica and further up the valley, and certainly on this side and sort of parts of the odd house in Santici towards our U.N. transport base here, was literally in flames, there was smoke pouring from houses all the way up Pirici, past Ahmici. As I went past here, which is a cemetery, down the hill and turned right, there were a line of bodies, about four or five men and women in a line lying dead here, and I pushed on, and I can't actually remember how far I went, maybe as far as the Busovaca junction or even further round towards the Jelinak junction, at which point I turned round, came back, and decided on the way back that I would visit the two commanders in Vitez and try and find out what on earth was going on. I went first, I think, to the HVO brigade commander in the cinema close to the Hotel Vitez, Commander Mario Chekhof's (sic) headquarters, and I met him there and we discussed what I had seen and what was going on, and he just kept telling me the situation was very confused. I had already gained --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a minute, if I might? Based on the reports you had received from your reconnaissance units as well as your personal observation from driving through the Lasva Valley and seeing the kinds of destruction that you saw, did you come to a preliminary conclusion as to what, in fact, was going on in the Lasva Valley on the morning of April 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and I confronted Commander Chekhof with that. It appeared to me to be a pre-emptive attack by the HVO forces down the length and breadth of the Lasva Valley against Muslim villages and Muslim forces and had certainly taken them, the Muslims and ourselves, by surprise, and that was evident when I spoke with Sefkija Bilic, the BiH commander in Stari Vitez, who was actually in a state of shock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you saw bodies. Do you have an idea of about how many bodies you saw on that quick tour through the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 20 or 30 bodies either on the road or in the fields and outside the houses, and the one thing that -- everlasting expression was the fact that they were all civilians, none of them were in uniform, which was quite shocking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they of both sexes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, men and women and children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw no children in Vitez. We saw children further down here, lying in the fields.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Further down toward the Ahmici area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, on this side here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pointing then to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the sort of -- the area of Ahmici and Pirici that are adjacent to the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned, I believe, seeing four bodies near the cemetery. Did anything about the way those four bodies were arranged give you pause for thought or indicate anything to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think the witness said seven or eight. I may have got that -- that was in Stari Vitez. How many bodies was it outside the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Outside the cemetery, there were about -- I think it was four, sir, four or five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Four. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were at the bottom of the driveway of a house, and they were in a line, they weren't covered, although later in the day, when I went past them again, someone had put blankets over them, but they were just lying there in a neat line. I mean, they had been laid out as a statement -- I mean, I don't know. But the impact, certainly on my soldiers, was quite shocking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There may be some confusion which I would like to, if we can, clarify. Those four bodies laid out along the side of the road were across from the cemetery, but you had seen other bodies as well during your tour through the Lasva Valley; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We had seen bodies off the road. These -- within Vitez, and these particular bodies were literally right beside my vehicle. That's why their impact was a bit greater.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I take it you did not actually get out of your vehicle and do a foot search of any of these areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't. There was a lot of small arms fire, and I decided that wasn't a prudent thing to do at that time. I did dismount from my vehicle when we returned to Vitez to visit the two headquarters. In fact, my Warrior took several bullet strikes during that morning, not that we were in any particular danger because it's a very well-protected vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But certainly another reason not to leave --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a good reason not to look out the top or leave it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Colonel Watters. You may resume your seat. Now, I believe you were telling us about meeting with the HVO commanders. I believe you mentioned his name as Cerkez, I think is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell us what happened there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to his headquarters with the liaison officer responsible for liaising with him, Commander Dundas Whattley ^, and had a discussion with him about what was going on and asked him to call his forces back and to stop attacking because, you know, it was obvious to us that it was the Croat HVO who were doing the attacking, and he agreed to meet at noon or so in our headquarters and have a cease-fire conference with the Muslim forces, which we arranged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the days that followed, did you participate in a series of cease-fire conferences that were less than satisfactory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The cease-fire conference at 12.00 that day didn't change anything despite the fact that we signed bits of paper and agreed to a cease-fire and a moving back of forces, exchanging of prisoners, retrieving of wounded. It made no difference at all, nor did the one on the morning of the 17th, which Colonel Stewart chaired. It was after that first conference at 12.00 on the 16th that we decided we actually had to act, and it was at that point that we started sending off patrols into the villages to extract the civilians, imposing a cease-fire by force of arms and extracting the civilians from the battle zones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was essentially at that point that the mission's thrust that we talked about the other day shifted, to some extent, from delivering humanitarian aid and support in that regard to actually becoming more active in protecting civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had never thought about it in those terms, but if you're looking for a transitory period, that is probably it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself return to Ahmici on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't. On the 16th, I, following the initial peace or cease-fire conference, one of the requirements of the BiH for agreeing to a cease-fire was that the wounded that they had in Kruscica were retrieved. They had no doctors in Kruscica and no means to treat their wounded, and they asked if we would evacuate the wounded from Kruscica, and that was agreed by the HVO forces, and I led a patrol into Kruscica on the night of the 16th to retrieve the wounded from Kruscica and take them to a Muslim medical facility in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would like to draw your attention -- before I ask you that question ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I could just add something to that, actually? Although there was fighting in the length and breadth of the valley, and by the late period of the 16th, it was very sporadic small arms fire and burning houses in the majority of the valley, the main concentrations of fighting were in -- and resistance by the BiH forces were in Kruscica and in Vitez, and it was there that we, from a command perspective, concentrated our efforts whilst using what resources we had, as I said earlier, to go into the villages in the valley and extract wounded and anyone essentially that we could find who needed help.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to direct your attention to two days later, April 18th. Were you in the ops room in your Vitez headquarters on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For periods of time, I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall anything unusual happening on that day in Stari Vitez? If not unusual, at least remarkable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, a quite catastrophic event, in our thinking. We had reports of a large explosion in Vitez, close to the mosque, in Stari Vitez. We didn't know initially what had caused the explosion, and I sent "A" Company down into Vitez to report what had happened, and they reported that there had been a large vehicle-borne improvised explosive device, VBID, had exploded within the centre of Vitez, and that there were approximately 30 homes destroyed. I think about -- at that point, we thought there were six people dead, eight people very seriously injured, and a further number of people injured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned VBID. Could you tell us what that is again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a weapon invented by the provisional IRA in Northern Ireland in the early '70s, and what it is, in colloquial terms, is a car or lorry bomb, a vehicle packed with explosives and a detonating device that is a weapon of terror.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "weapon of terror"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a weapon employed in our -- up till then, in our experience, in my personal experience, in Northern Ireland, was a weapon deployed by terrorists to break the will of the people, to terrorise the people, kill and maim the people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would be the purpose of a terrorist bomb in Vitez on the date of April 18, in your view as a military man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a stalemate in the fighting. The BiH forces in Vitez and Kruscica were still holding out. The BiH third corps were beginning to consolidate themselves and beginning to mount a counterattack, and I think the VBID was deployed into Stari Vitez to effect an outcome in the stalemate. I think it was the act of quite desperate people to deploy such an indiscriminate bomb into a heavily populated area, and designed like any weapon of terror, to terrorise and to drive the people out of the town, which it succeeded in doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which people was it intended to drive out of town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The civilian population -- well, I mean, anybody, but it's the civilian population who were most traumatised by it, although so were the military. About 130 people were made homeless, having had their houses destroyed, and about 400 people that evening left Stari Vitez and sought sanctuary at our logistic base outside of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again Stari Vitez was almost an exclusively Muslim area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Almost -- at that point it was almost an exclusively Muslim area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned acts of terror intended to send a message. Was there another act of terror on the following day, on the 19th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was. There was the firing of, I think, eight rounds of heavy calibre artillery into the middle of Zenica, which I would describe as slightly more strategic terrorism.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The weapon that was used in Vitez could have been assembled by anyone with the knowledge and expertise. The firing of heavy calibre artillery within the HVO was controlled at the highest levels, and to fire eight rounds into Vitez would have been a deliberate act by the HVO regional command as opposed to a weapon of terror, which could have been deployed at any level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us a sense of the distance that the shells were fired from into Vitez and also give us a sense of the size of the weapon that must have been used to accomplish that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't assemble any proof as to exactly what weapon fired it, but our U.N. investigators who went into Vitez said it was a heavy calibre artillery piece, and it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt again, Mr. Moskowitz. The witness said the weapons were fired into Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's now talking about Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, did I say Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Maybe we should clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you again, if you would, clarify the target of this attack on the 19th and describe the nature of that target, if you could, and give us a sense of the general area from which the shelling took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The target on the 19th was the largely Muslim town of Zenica which was the headquarters of the third BiH corps, and it was that corps, on the 19th, that had extracted itself from its missions in the east in support of the Muslim pockets and had moved itself and reconfigured itself for a counterattack against the HVO in the Lasva Valley. And the eight rounds of heavy artillery that fell on Zenica which caused quite a few people to be killed, I can't remember the exact number, was -- we had reports of certain large HVO-controlled artillery pieces, one known as Nora which was in a quarry not far from ourselves which we heard fire, and the firing in the same time frame of the heavy calibre 150-millimetre sort of artillery pieces of the HVO and the impacting of the rounds in Zenica correlated, I mean we can never prove which gun fired those rounds, but we were in no doubt that it was HVO artillery, and it was a message to the Muslim third corps and the Muslim BiH forces that if they continued to prosecute their counterattack, then the HVO would flatten Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, just to orient everyone, Zenica would be the large town at the end of that mountain road that you pointed out yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be about where the door is on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if you follow that mountain road to the door, you'd be in Zenica, is what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a fairly large town of about 100.000 people or so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a large old steel town during the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, prior to April 22nd, and I want to direct your attention to that date, now. Prior to April 22nd, had you focused on the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From a command point of view, no. We had had Warrior patrols go to Ahmici, and one particular patrol brought back, I think, 16 women and children who they evacuated under fire. These people were carried behind a bank of earth and the Warrior reversed up to the bank of earth, opened the rear doors, the soldiers got out and got I think up to 16 women and children in the back of the Warrior and we took them to Travnik. That was one incidents that stands out. We had had reports that people had been in Ahmici, but we had reports that people had been killed in all the Muslim villages in the Lasva Valley. And we had reports of atrocities committed by Muslim forces against Croats and Croat villages, which we also investigated. And we had found dead bodies in some of these Croat villages, but not on the scale we found in the Muslim villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be true to say that one of the reasons that, prior to April 22nd, the village of Ahmici did not draw your attention during those tragic times was because your information was that there was really no BiH army in Ahmici or in the immediate environs of Ahmici, in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The two centres of BiH military that we were aware of were in Vitez and in Kruscica. We were unaware of any concentrations of BiH forces in any other villages. There were soldiers returning from front-line service who lived in these villages, but there weren't military installations in those villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Barracks, that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. And that was evident in the fact that there was no fighting in those villages. The fighting occurred very violently on the morning of the 16th, and other than Kruscica and Vitez it got quiet, other than sort of odd burning houses and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did it come about that on April 22nd you first became aware of atrocities in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 21st I chaired another cease-fire conference, this one in shadow of high-level negotiations between the head of the armies of the armies of the BiH and the HVO. And we held a high level conference in Bila school headed up by the chiefs of staff of the BiH and the HVO, General Petkovic from the HVO and General Halilovic from the BiH. We had a cease-fire agreement based on the creation of a demilitarised zone either side of the Lasva Valley road from which the HVO would draw back into Vitez and Busovaca and the BiH would withdraw approximately, I think it was six or seven kilometres from the road parallel with the mountain road towards Zenica and create this buffer zone which we would control and keep the two warring factions apart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you for a moment there. The BiH army you are describing was an army that had come into the valley in response to what had happened on the 16th, the attack on Vitez and the Lasva Valley; is that your information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, commander third corps BiH, Hadzjhasanovic, I think he was, had picked up his corps and moved it some considerable distance over a couple of days and redeployed it in a counter attack from Zenica down the mountain road and looping around to link up with his forces in Kruscica. At that point on the 21st the BiH counter attack had pushed back the HVO, essentially into two pockets; one pocket into Busovaca and one in Vitez, and completely turned the tables on the HVO. And the HVO at that point were in defence and the BiH were conducting a very successful counteroffensive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Counteroffensive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The third army was not in the Lazva Valley on April 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Third corps, the elements of third corps in Vitez and Kruscica, if you look up the chain of command, but the actual main centre of the corps were not, they were east towards Srebrenica and Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Busy with the Serb campaign?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Continue, now, as to how you found out about or discovered the atrocities that occurred in Ahmici on April 22nd.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Having put together the cease-fire agreement and signed up to it, and facilitated the two commanders, visiting their front-line soldiers to brief them on the cease-fire, which we did using our own vehicles, we had said that the following morning we would deploy a patrol which Colonel Stewart would lead that would confirm the withdrawal of the BiH and HVO forces. The reality was that the BiH had to do a considerable withdrawal, because they had made considerable gains in their counter attack and were actually on the Lazva Valley road and had captured the key junctions on the road. They really had to withdraw. The HVO had little withdrawing to do because they were forced into their two pockets. So the emphasis was to go and police the withdrawal of the BiH forces and ensure they were signing up to their agreement; because the consequences of them attacking Vitez and the other HVO positions were quite catastrophic in terms of the strategic situation in Bosnia at that time. And if Busovaca and Vitez had been taken by the BiH, the potential sort of total war within central Bosnia was almost certain. And there were large reinforcements coming up from Prozor of HVO forces, and it was important to stop the war before they joined against third corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was a withdrawal agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was. And on the morning of the 22nd, Colonel Stewart led a patrol of himself, reconnaissance elements from our cavalry squadron, and elements from our Royal Engineer squadron to go and police the lines of withdrawal. And when he got to the hills above Ahmici there were still groups of BiH forces from third corps who refused to withdraw, and they told him that they wouldn't withdraw because of the massacre of women and children in Ahmici. And Colonel Stewart and ourselves were unaware of a massacre in Ahmici. We knew people had been killed in Ahmici, and we had effected evacuation of people of Ahmici, but we didn't know of a massacre. Colonel Stewart thought it was a slight exaggeration and said he would go down and personally check Ahmici and assure them there had not been a massacre there. And he then went from there into Ahmici where he did discover a number of bodies and the evidence of possible, of a possible massacre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This would have been sometime during the morning of April 22nd?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then have an opportunity to speak with Colonel Stewart later that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel Stewart came back to our headquarters, and he and ambassador Thebault, who was the United Nations ambassador who had been with Colonel Stewart, they were both extremely shaken and angry at what they had seen. And having Colonel Stewart describe to me what he had seen I felt I had to visit myself as his second in command, so I understood why my commanding officer was in the state he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall some of the things he told you he saw in Ahmici that made him and the ambassador so shaken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The scale of the destruction of the village. And in one particular, and he described seeing parts of a skull and that sort of thing in houses, and he also believed that there were bodies in all the houses because the houses had been systematically destroyed and the roofs dropped. And it was his belief, after seeing one particular house, that there were dozens of bodies under the roofs of these houses that he wasn't able to see. And he drew that conclusion from a particular house that had not been destroyed in which there were about seven or so, six or seven bodies, which had been burned and were in a hideous state. And it was the sight of that and the extrapolation of that to the rest of the village that had caused him to be so shocked and angry. And to be absolutely fair, as well, we felt a sense of personal failure as a unit that this had happened in the area that we were responsible for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I would ask the usher, who I think had just left the courtroom, but we would like to set up the easel to show exhibit number 5, which is the enlargement of Ahmici, excuse me, exhibit number 2, the enlargement of Ahmici, and ask Colonel Watters to indicate the route he took on April 22nd when he arrived in that village. With the permission of the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Watters could you approach the exhibit, and this is an enlargement of the area of Ahmici, Santici and Nadioci, and could you show the Court the route that you took into Ahmici on April 22nd?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I took my Warriors and drove out of our school, came past Vitez on the ring road and down to the junction here, turned left, went past the large minaret that had been blown up on the mosque here, and then drove up to this point here, which I don't remember being as large as this, we called it sort of a turning circle. And in my past experience this was the sort of upper reaches of Ahmici, and as far as I had ever been in Ahmici. When we got here it was, there were two things; one was the stark contrast having driven up where the destroyed houses were, there were a series of houses here that were untouched by the fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just for the record, so we can have it clear, you're taking your pointer and drawing a circle around the houses surrounding the turn around point, essentially in the centre of the area map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you said that turn around point was not as large in 1993 as it appears on the map in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was probably a quarter of the size, just sort of here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, if you would, could you describe the sort of stark contrast within that circle and without that circle or outside of that circle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The contrast, as we would come up here, having been through devastation, we then arrived in normality again, there were normal Bosnian houses, and they had not been involved in fighting. And Colonel Stewart had told me that the house he had found the bodies in was beyond these houses, further up into upper Ahmici. I had never been up there before. I decided we would dismount here, at that point we came under sniper fire from this area here. The rounds were going over our heads, it wasn't my deduction they were trying to kill us, it was my deduction they were trying to frighten us away. So I sent a patrol up here to clear out the snipers. They didn't make contact, and just I positioned counter-snipers here while we conducted a foot patrol around this area just to have a look at it. And it was this area that I believed our previous extraction of civilians from Ahmici had taken place, and I was interested to have a look at the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you for one moment to clarify, again, the record. Sniper fire was coming from just outside the perimeter of that circle you had drawn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is high wooded ground here and there was sniper fire coming from the high ground over our heads. It stopped when we deployed our soldiers up there and the snipers withdrew, we never actually saw them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I conducted a patrol around here, and began to, from the evidence I saw on the ground, such as positions that had obviously been occupied by soldiers where the grass had been flattened down and there were empty cases 7.62 long, which is the sort of sniper round from a sniper rifle. There were positions that made it obvious to us that there had been, using our tactical doctrine and superimposing it on the sign we saw on the ground, there was a series of cut off positions; soldiers occupying positions to either stop people infiltrating or stop people exfiltrating from the operation to attack the village. I then, having walked around here and seen no evidence of any bodies -- .

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Slow down a little bit so our translators and interpreters can keep up. Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We then mounted Warrior vehicles again and moved up the village moved past the mosque, which was also destroyed in this area here, and parked the vehicles about here, dismounted again and conducted another foot patrol in this area and found the house that Colonel Stewart had described to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you describe what you saw at that house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were a series of steps leading up to a, sort of front door, and on the steps there was a small burned body which obviously looked like a child. And behind, I think, or beside that body was a larger body of an adult, also burned really beyond recognition, other than it was a large body. The rest of the first floor of the house was completely wrecked, but there were no more bodies. We then went down into the cellar where there was it was quite-- there were bodies, you could see the shapes of the skulls, the rib cages, and they were in a line by one of the cellar walls and they had been burned, and there was evidence of a petrol can or some sort of thing down there. And there were -- Colonel Stewart had described to me his belief was these people, from the way the bodies were positioned, had been burned alive in the cellar. I made a careful examination of the cellar and found bullet marks on the rear of the cellar, it looked like from the grouping they were from an automatic weapon, and also what appeared to be blood running down the cellar walls, and deduced from it that probably the people had been not been burned alive but had been shot in the cellar and then burned. And although that sounds a strange academic thing to be concerned with at that time, I wanted to be able to go back to my CO and assure him that the people had not been burnt alive, because that had deeply upset him. We then went back up to the top of the village to turn the Warriors around and there was total devastation. There was not a house that had not been destroyed. They had been systematically destroyed, there was not the scene of battle the likes of which we had seen in Vitez and my own military experience in other parts of the world. There were not rocket grenade explosions on the walls, no great heaps of empty cases, there weren't dead soldiers or the signs of where dead soldiers had been, blood and so on. The thing that was shocking was that the village was totally destroyed, the animals were destroyed, the crop, the root cellars, everything was destroyed. There was nothing to come back to that village for. We came back down the road and stopped again at the turning circle here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This, again, is that area -- I don't want to mischaracterise your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The island of normality in a sea of destruction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was those sort of analogies. I was just trying to make sense of it. I never thought of the ethnic composition of villages in Bosnia, it wasn't something we focused on. We were delivering aid to people who needed it, it didn't matter who they were, and we were on nobody's side. I stopped because I just wanted to clear in my own mind why there was this completely untouched area of the village when the remainder of the village was utterly destroyed. And it was if a forest fire had swept through a forest, and for some reason there was a small stand of trees in the middle that had not been touched, and that was very curious. Why hadn't they all been destroyed. And I went and banged on a door of a house opposite where the Warrior was, we could see people moving around, curtains moving and so on. No one would come out and talk to us. I asked them to come out and tell us what they had seen. We assumed these people had been witnesses to what had taken place. And no one would come out and talk to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, if I may interrupt. Did you, yourself, actually go up to that house by the turn around and bang on the door yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With a couple of my soldiers, and a couple of soldiers went behind that house to other houses and banged on the doors as well, we shouted at the people in the houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall what you were shouting, what were you saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Come out and talk to us, what's happening here, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a loud voice so it could be heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, shouting at the people through the glass. We could see them moving around in the house, they wouldn't come out and talk to us. It became obvious as we were talking among ourselves and with our interpreters, who were from the local areas and had a deeper understanding than ourselves of the ethnic mix of people in the village, that these houses belonged to Croat people whereas the remainder of the village was Muslim. And we knew it was Muslim because it had a mosque and minaret. We didn't realise there were parts that were not Muslim until then. So, guilt by association really, these people were spared and the rest of the village was destroyed and the people killed. And extrapolating as Colonel Stewart had done, our fear was that beneath the roofs of the houses were more bodies like the one in the upper village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you in fact do an additional foot search looking for more evidence of atrocities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were one or two houses that had been destroyed and we went in those, and I have a vivid memory of a rib cage in one of them. I couldn't tell if it was a human ribcage or not, I mean, it looked human but I'm not a doctor. And further down in this part of the village I think there was a skull, a human skull in one of the houses. They were the only signs of dead people we had physically seen. In the upper village the house with all the bodies in it, and then a rib cage and a skull. But as I said, you couldn't really examine most of the houses because the roof had dropped inside the walls of the house, covering everything inside the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Could you resume taking your seat. At this time I would ask the usher to show the witness three photographs, in that order. If you would place that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 10.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, could you look at that photograph, exhibit 10, and describe what that is, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what we used to call the Ahmici mosque. You could see it from the main Lasva Valley road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that what you saw when you entered the village of Ahmici on April 22nd?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Although, I had vivid memories when the minaret was standing, as well, earlier in the month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we show the next photograph, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution exhibit number 11.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, Colonel, if you would describe what that picture displays?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's again a closer picture of the Ahmici mosque taken from the road that ran sort of parallel to the main Lasva Valley road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that accurately describes what you saw on April 22nd, with respect to that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the way out of Ahmici we went down and examined the mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you examined the mosque did you look at the minaret in particular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, the minaret had been made of reinforced concrete, and you could see the reinforcing struts which were shiny, and it had recently been blown down. It was demolished, it was a clinical, efficient demolition. I mean, it hadn't been knocked over or sort of shot over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What led you to the conclusion it had been demolished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a reinforced concrete structure, and when you looked at base of it, it had been blown up by someone that knew what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we show the next photo?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution exhibit number 12.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 12 has been placed on the ELMO, Colonel, does this illustrate what you are talking about regarding the minaret being demolished or blown up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what I saw. Again, without making too much of the point, again, it was shocking, it was an act of sacrilege against a religious building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you mentioned in your earlier testimony that you had also seen the destruction of a mosque further down the road past the turnaround point in upper Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It hadn't been blown up like this, it didn't have a minaret. It had been sort of destroyed like the other houses; the roof had been dropped into the building and the building had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 13.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, this next photograph, Exhibit 13, again describe what that is, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the smaller mosque further into the upper part of Ahmici village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that picture illustrate what you saw that day, or has there been additional damage done to what you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not exactly as I remember it. I mean -- I remember the building had been destroyed. I remember it as having the walls intact but no roof and all the windows showing inside had been burnt and gutted. I don't remember the walls collapsed. They might have been. It's not an image that sticks in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Show the next photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's an aerial shot of the same building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The upper mosque?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The upper mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And that would be Exhibit 14.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: We are now going to tender a series of photographs depicting the cellar of the house. These photographs are, some of them, quite graphic, and I just want to alert those who will look at it that they are quite graphic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, could you quickly describe --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- what is now placed on the ELMO as --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel switch on his microphone?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Prosecution Exhibit number 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, could you describe what Exhibit 15 shows, now having been placed on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I took a series of photographs, I don't know if this is one of them, of the building in the upper part of the town that we found the bodies in. This is in the cellar of that building, and you can see one of the bodies, the skull of one of the bodies, sort of arched back, and other parts of bodies in this area here. This is the skull. And just at the back, you can see what I believe was blood running down the walls, and just above that blood, there is -- in fact, you can see one right there -- a series of bullet marks in the wall, and it appeared that the people had been lined up here and then shot, and they fell in a heap here, and then they were burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Can you place the next photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 16.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That last picture I believe was this area over here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. The witness's microphone is not switched on. The witness's microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The previous photograph was in this area here (indicating), and this is further along the line of bodies, this is another skull and parts of the body here, and there were -- it was difficult to tell, but there were four or so bodies there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: The next photograph, please, Mr. Usher?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 17.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exhibit 17.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the first floor of the house, as you come up the steps here, and this is the larger of the two bodies I earlier described lying just above the steps leading into the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is not in the basement but at the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this is not in the basement. This is at the top of the stairs leading into the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it would be in view of people who were walking by that house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, we saw that and the smaller body actually from the -- sort of the garden of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: May we have the next photograph, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 18.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, now, does this photograph provide a little more information on the bullet holes in the wall that you saw and the blood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. You can see parts of the bodies here, there's part of the rib cage, and behind here is the cluster of bullet marks and what we presumed to be blood here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And the next photograph, if you would, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 19.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell us what is going on here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are members of the medical section and stretcher bearers who were actually a band from the 1 Cheshire BRITBAT clearing the bodies from the cellar at a later date, I think it was the 27th of April, when no one else seemed to have moved the bodies and the commanding officer made the decision that we should, and we contacted an imam who came and performed a religious ceremony, and then under his supervision, we removed the bodies, and they were taken to Zenica for burial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zenica would be where the hospital was, the morgue; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Well, there was one in Travnik as well, but the Muslim authorities, religious authorities, asked us if we would help escort the bodies to Zenica, which we said we would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Next photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 20.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is Exhibit 20, I believe. Again, quickly, we are seeing what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's in the cellar of the house on the same day, the same people removing another body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Next photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 21.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Twenty-one, again --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same cellar and our soldiers removing bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Next and final photograph of this series.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 22.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the smaller of the two bodies on the first floor, on the steps sort of leading up towards the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Moskowitz, are we moving from those photographs?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It might be a convenient moment to deal with this. From the point of view of clarification during the rest of the trial, that house has been referred to as the house where Colonel Stewart found the bodies. Now, for the rest of the trial, clearly we're going to need to know which house that is, which house the Prosecution, at least, say it is. Which house is it? Can you clarify that for us so we can make a note?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, we can clarify it, but I will tell the Court it will not play a major role in the rest of the trial in terms of incidents that we are going to present during the rest of the trial, so it may not be necessary to do that, but we can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It occurs to me, while we're on this subject, that there will, no doubt, be a number of houses which are going to be referred to by different witnesses, and we will need to know which houses it's said they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes. And we will, as you see and as we proceed in this trial, have a series of exhibits where houses will be referred to by number and by letter as well as the names assigned to those houses, and those numbers and letters will be consistent from witness to witness, so that I think, as we proceed, the Court will become quite familiar with the relevant and important houses that we will be focusing on in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As soon as possible. I would find it helpful to have a plan with those houses identified and this house in particular.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, you mentioned the commander, Stewart, arriving in Ahmici on the 22nd, before you did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are aware that a videotape was made of that visit, are you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am, sir. He had a media team with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we, at this moment, ask that the video, which would be our next exhibit, be played, and as we are watching that video, and it's a fairly short one, if you would, Colonel, just give us a narrative of what we are seeing and where we are in Ahmici as the video is being played, if you can. Yes, if you would, Colonel, what do we see here? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are two British battalion soldiers. That's a picture of the mosque there in Ahmici. They're either Royal Engineers or 9/12 Lancers, I don't know which they are, but they're certainly British battalion. Again, the mosque in lower Ahmici, the minaret. That's one of our CVRT vehicles, that's something called a 432. That's the large body at the house. That's the smaller body, probably a child. More shots of the same bodies. Again, the smaller body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's happening here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are Royal Engineers who are checking for mines, for landmines or booby traps on the routes around the house before Colonel Stewart's party would have actually gone up to the house. Mines were a constant threat. We had many soldiers injured from mines during our tour there. That's one of our CVRT command vehicles. That's the same vehicle. That's the vehicle driver. That's an ammunition box. That's an empty shell case. Just general scenes of Ahmici village, the upper part of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was some sniper activity that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was. These soldiers are pointing at where shots had come from and they're trying to pin down where the snipers are shooting from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what this is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the mosque in upper Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you stop there for a minute? Can we stop it now? Could we reverse and go back to the big white house? Can we reverse and go back to the big white house? Right there. No, too far. That's it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this house appear to be similar to the one that you knocked on the door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it looks like the house that faced the turning circle. It was one of the houses that, in stark contrast to the other houses, had not been damaged at all and it still stood and was occupied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you mentioned the sort of circle of houses that were undamaged, and then outside the circle, houses were damaged. Do you see the house --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- behind the undamaged house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is a damaged house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that people were scurrying around inside this house while you were knocking on it and telling them to come out and talk to you, do you recall where in that house you noticed curtains moving and people about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just in the windows, certainly on the ground floor, I remember seeing the curtains move and go back again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice any damage whatsoever to that house by the turning circle when you went up to it and knocked on the door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see any damage, I don't remember seeing any damage, and proportionately to the rest of the village, which was destroyed, they appeared to be untouched.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know this video is not the clearest picture in the world, but do you see any damage on this image of this house taken on April 22nd?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing -- no, I can see no damage to it at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You can proceed. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you mentioned dead animals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is one -- the thing that was so appalling is that everything was destroyed, sheep, cattle, everything, and there were dead animals all over the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see a dog there. Did you notice whether the dogs were, in any way -- well, I don't know how to put this delicately -- but involved with any of the corpses that you had seen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the reasons that we wanted to take action to remove the corpses, was as the days progressed, the corpses were obviously being eaten by dogs or other wildlife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Watters, based on everything you had seen during the time period between the 16th of April and the 22nd of April and everything you had heard, and in particular based on what you had seen and observed in the village of Ahmici, could you tell us, as a military professional, what in your view had, in fact, occurred in Ahmici on April 16th and 17th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The village, which didn't appear to be defended, had been systematically destroyed in a quite ruthlessly efficient military operation. The surrounds of the village, if you like, had been cordoned, soldiers had been placed in cut-offs and we deduced that from where we had seen the grass pressed down and the empty cases from rifles, and then a house-clearing operation, as we would describe it, had been conducted, and people had been killed in their houses or had fled their houses, and then simultaneously and subsequently, all the houses had been burned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not all, though.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the houses had been burnt apart from, as I described earlier, what we later understood to be Croat houses in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did that distinction between the houses that had been destroyed, the vast majority had been destroyed and the few that had not, give you an indication of the kind of operation this really was on April 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We knew it was a Croat offensive that had taken place, an HVO offensive, and we deduced later why it had happened, and why it had happened then from the circumstances surrounding it. It was a ruthless operation, and we later came to understand why Ahmici had possibly be selected for specifically savage and total destruction; in that it was a centre within the Lasva Valley, and indeed within the Muslim psyche of Bosnia, it was quite a special place and the best parallel I can probably draw is Guca Gora which is a Croat village which had a similar significance to the Croat peoples, and Ahmici provided a large number of religious leaders to the Muslim faith within Bosnia, larger than its population would suggest, so a disproportionate number of young men from this village had become Muslim imams and teachers. This is something we didn't know until afterwards, and it made it a particularly important target to the concept of ethnically cleansing the Muslim people from the Lasva Valley, I mean, it was a -- it was used, we believed, as an example as to what would happen if you didn't leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not perhaps dissimilar to the truck bomb earlier in Vitez, an example of terror?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It certainly was an example of terror. One of the things that did puzzle us later when we discovered that the majority of the dead from Ahmici had been taken to Vitez and we later buried a hundred of those or helped the authorities in Vitez bury them on the 28th, I think it was, of April, why that particular house had been left, whether it had been left as a deliberate sign of ritualistic terror or whether it had just been overlooked, we never knew, but it certainly was shocking and it certainly shocked my soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say and conclude then that your view of what had happened at Ahmici was that this was a systematic and organised attempt to ethnically cleanse that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in absolutely no doubt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have an idea as to why it happened then, on April 16th, that these systematic attacks occurred throughout the Lasva Valley by the HVO? Why then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was the motive and there was the opportunity, when one analysed it. The motive was to ethnically cleanse the Muslim minority from the largely Croat future canton ten as part of the Vance-Owen Plan which was a copy cat technique that the Serbs at that time were employing in Eastern Bosnia against the Muslim minorities there. Secondly, we believed that it was tied into a wider plan to secure a Croat-controlled route from Prozor around through Gornji Vakuf up through Vitez to Kiseljak via the Kiseljak valley. And the securing of that route had strategic implications with the development of the Vance-Owen Plan and the ability of the Serbs and the Muslims to close the main arterial roads through the country which were blocked by the Serbs and by the Muslim forces down in Mostar -- yes, I mean Mostar, and so they were the reasons. The opportunity, the imminence of the possibility of the Vance-Owen Plan being a settlement and being imposed on Central Bosnia, and from a strategic military point of view the Muslim forces were totally focused on the war with the Serbs in eastern Bosnia and the media equally were nowhere to be seen in the Lasva Valley. They were all in Tuzla watching the quite dreadful scenes of the refugees coming out of Srbrenica, and there was a window of opportunity. We hadn't identified this before, and we had no inkling that the Croats had an aspiration to secure ethnically their part of Central Bosnia until, you know, the 16th and 17th of April. It wasn't a spontaneous -- in the past, we had seen at the village level, the tactical level, disagreements between opposing cultural and ethnic groups spark up into conflict, and this is initially what we thought it was until we understood the scale of it with the use of mortars and artillery, and the other confirmation of that hypothesis which we were putting together -- I was putting together in our information cell over the next few days, was the coordination of the attacks throughout the valley and also in Prozor and to the east of Prozor, to the Muslim villages there, where there was a road that the bypass Gornji Vakuf and could put through from Prozor straight across to north of Kiseljak and Busovaca into the back of Busovaca, and it appeared that the HVO were trying to sort of push across from north of Prozor to Busovaca and also, having essentially secured Gornji Vakuf, they were securing the areas of possible BiH interdiction of their arterial route into canton ten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to summarise your testimony, and tell me if this is fair or not, that while the world and the BiH army was looking elsewhere, the HVO took an opportunity to ethnically cleanse the Lasva Valley in anticipation of the Vance-Owen Plan coming into effect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, and that was further illustrated by the suing for peace over the period 18th, 19th, 20th, of the HVO at the strategic as well as the operational level which involved the HVO not giving up their gains but imposing a cease-fire at the status quo of HVO gains, and this was initially supported by Izetbegovic at sort of the strategic level of the Muslim people but rejected at the operational level because the operational commanders realised that their position was totally untenable, and until they had re-established their former lines and re-secured their villages, they had no intention of suing for peace, and it was that conflict of aspiration that later led us to understand why the series of peace initiatives that we negotiated up until the 21st, you know, had no chance of ever happening, really, they were just placating the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I just have, I think, one or two very short areas to get into. I know we're at the 11.00 hour. I don't anticipate this will take more than five minutes, ten minutes, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Earlier in your testimony, you had pointed out for us the Dubravica school, and I want you to tell us briefly what you remember on a particular day during this time period when you were travelling over the mountain road and noticed something unusual around the Dubravica school area, if you would?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was travelling on the mountain road, and out of the Dubravica school came a column of men and boys, some of whom had their hands tied behind their backs, they looked like a prisoner column, and they had -- some of them were also carrying spades and pick axes and they were guarded by HVO soldiers, and they were moving up the mountain road towards what we knew were the HVO forward positions on the mountain road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you suspect that perhaps something was going on at the Dubravica school that needed to be looked into?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, I deduced that the HVO were using the Dubravica school as a prison camp and that my deduction was that these prisoners were being taken to dig trenches which is a contravention of the Geneva Convention to use prisoners for such things, and on my return, I reported that to the ICRC, the -- the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's your information that the ICRC then went into the Dubravica school and essentially negotiated a release of Muslims who were kept prisoner in that school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, a delegate from the ICRC visited the Dubravica school and over a series of protracted negotiations secured the release of prisoners from that school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning to a little different area, you mentioned earlier about the burial in Stari Vitez or in Vitez of the victims from the Lasva Valley attack, many of whom were from Ahmici. Could you tell us what you know about that burial and how that came about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were aware that the HVO and Vitez authorities had an improvised morgue in the school in Vitez, and we received a request, and I can't remember whether it came from the civil or the military authorities, if we would assist with the burying of up to 100 bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the problem with those bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a straight hygienic problem. They were in various stages of decomposition, and they were a considerable health threat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this on or about the 28th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was on the 28th of April, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it would be about twelve days after the attack in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. We sent our stretcher bearers and Royal Engineers and "A" company to Vitez to assist and, in reality, to actually dig a mass grave in a field beside Vitez and to lay the bodies in the grave with the help of the authorities and then fill it in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, during that time period, after the attacks on the valley, meeting a young girl by the name of Melissa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met her in Colonel Stewart's accommodation and she was in the company of two Red Cross delegates and I had been invited to Colonel Stewart's accommodation to join him for supper, and I was introduced to the -- I knew one of the Red Cross delegates, I was introduced to the other one, and a young girl about the same age as my own daughter, and she described how she had been in the village of Ahmici and it was actually very poignant and tragic that her mother and father and herself had been chased by soldiers and there was a lot of noise and everyone lay down on the grass, were made to get down on the grass, there was a lot of noise, and then her mother and father never got up again, and it's very tragic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then finally, Colonel, I think you mentioned the use of many different kinds of weapons during the attack on the Lasva Valley. During your stay there in Central Bosnia and in the Lasva Valley, did you have occasion to see anti-aircraft weapons placed on the back of flat bed trucks driven by HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, various types, some with two barrels, some with four barrels, some 20-millimetre, some up to 40-millimetre, and we were particularly interested in them because they were, to our point of view, they were combat indicators because they were weapons that were controlled at least at the operational level and not at the tactical level, so where they were indicated that something important was happening or was going to happen if they were deployed operationally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: If I might ask the usher one last time for this witness to ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The other point we were interested in them is they were one of the few weapons that we saw moderately regularly that we thought would actually penetrate our own armoured vehicles, so we were particularly concerned about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you would make it a point, if you could, to take photographs when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. I did and everyone was instructed to.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 24.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit 24, when it appears on the ELMO. There it is. Could you describe briefly what that is and whose weapon that appears to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I took a photograph of either this vehicle or one very similar to it in the Lasva Valley over that period. It is an HVO vehicle, and, in fact, in the photograph I originally had, you could quite plainly see the HVO badge on the number plate. It's a four-barrel anti-aircraft weapon mounted on a flatbed truck, and with a crew. They quite often had a trailer they towed with the ammunition in it as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a little difficult for me anyway to make out the four barrels. If you might point that out for the Court, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The barrels are sort of pointing sky ward here, one, two, three, four, that sort of area there (indicating) and so that's the actual weapon itself. The sandbags are probably used to stabilise the base of the weapon, and these are sort of soldiers that are crewing the weapon or protecting the weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would these be HVO soldiers, based on your experience?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was an HVO vehicle. They're HVO soldiers. I mean, in a better photograph, you'd probably be able to distinguish their cap badges and their badges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one last question. I'm a little confused as to why there was a need for an anti-aircraft weapon in Central Bosnia. Was there a serious threat of air attack from anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. These vehicles -- these weapons were mounted on vehicles in what we would describe as the direct fire row and so they were actually used against targets on the ground and I saw them actually firing and they are utterly devastating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are they fairly accurate weapon at distant ranges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At distant ranges the spread of them is considerable, at short ranges they are very accurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we're talking short range, what's a short range for highly accurate targeting of that weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not an expert, but from my observations of the weapon firing, up to about six or so hundred metres they are quite accurate. Their zone of fire is quite small. As you then get longer ranges, the zone of fire increases. The accuracy of zone of fire remains, but the area in which the rounds fall gets larger.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we take a break, may I ask a question to Mr. Pavkovic. Mr. Pavkovic, who is going to cross-examine the witness on behalf of various legal counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Defence would like to notify the Trial Chamber on two issues. First, we owe you our reply, and that is that the Defence will make opening statements after the Prosecution completes its case and before the beginning of the Defence case. Secondly, the Defence does not agree with the position that only one of the Defence counsel should carry out the cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses. It is the position of the Defence that that would infringe upon the rights of the Defence. Our position is as follows: When there are several accused on the same indictment, as we have in this case, the Defence believe that the right of each Defendant should not be impaired as a result, including the right to cross-examine. That is why the Defence would like to propose that it be given the chance for each Defence counsel to cross-examine each of the Prosecution witnesses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Let me respond right away. Actually, yesterday, I simply read out one of our guidelines where it is clear that the Defence may consider appointing one of them to cross-examine a particular witness, so we didn't say that you would have to appoint, in each case, only one legal counsel.
