utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw with my own eyes on a number of occasions Zoran Papic bringing in, in his own car, war material as well as Pero Papic. I even noticed that Pero Papic was very well-versed in military electronics, and I saw with my own eyes, when the truck came from the direction of Busovaca, and near Ivica Kupreskic's house, you can't see that on this photograph -- it is up here -- boxes with ammunition were unloaded, and it was placed in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you mention that weapons had to be surrendered by Muslims before they were allowed to return to their homes. Do you know whether, in fact, weapons were surrendered?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: The Bosniak inhabitants of Zume were deprived of all the weapons they had. They were seized from them. As far as I recall, an agreement was reached that four rifles should be surrendered to them and they, in fact, were. That was a condition. At first they demanded that all the weapons be surrendered, but our boys would not agree to that, and then they returned four rifles, and after that, they were allowed to go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: How many days or weeks after the conflict in 1992 were people beginning to return to their homes in that part of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: After about ten days. I just know that my family was among the last to return. No, maybe more days. But after a period of about ten days, some people started returning, I think that we went back about 20 days later or maybe a month on the outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: During the time period between the attack in '93 and the conflict in '92, did you see Dragan Papic in the village of Ahmici from time to time?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would see him, but I rarely had any contact with him. I remember something that might be of interest. I saw him in Zume with his brother Goran, he was carrying a sniper and wearing a military uniform, and he was even waving around a device for strangulation. It is a device with handles at both ends. It is flexible. And then you throw it around a person's neck, and that's how you choke him. He was carrying this and they were laughing, he and his brother. On the main road towards Rovna, I can't show you that junction here, he often carried a sniper. Sometimes he wore a black uniform, sometimes a camouflage uniform, sometimes he was in civilians clothes, but in any event he was there, he was living there in our settlement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness says carrying a sniper. Would you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: By "sniper," what do you mean, Mr. Ahmic, when you saw Mr. Papic, Dragan Papic, carrying a sniper, what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Dragan Papic carried a sniper rifle to show off and to intimidate people. I told you that it was quite astonishing to me that he suddenly had an interest in weapons. I don't think he was on duty because sniper is a device with sights that you target from a distance, and so he was carrying it around mostly to publicise the fact that he had one in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And you mention that you saw him carrying a strangling device as well as the sniper rifle. What do you mean by that, if you could clarify that for us as well?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: It's a device which has two handles at each end and a flex is threaded through it and it is very handy if you want to strangle somebody with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, did you ever see, in addition to that, any weapons in and around Dragan Papic's house in this time period that we're talking about between the two conflicts?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me mention a detail that I eye-witnessed. He would pass -- a truck would pass along this road with a heavy weapon on it, a four-barrelled anti-aircraft gun or machine gun, and Dragan Papic would call these people to stop by in his yard and Dragan Papic would climb on this anti-aircraft gun and he would fire in the air and above the houses, but for intimidation purposes. As far as I remember he didn't damage anything, but it was all meant as some kind of a provocation, using this weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, I want to direct your attention, Mr. Ahmic, to the night before the attack on Ahmici in April. Do you recall where you were that night, on April 15, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I went to my uncle's with my brother Muris, here (indicating) marked with number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you're indicating --

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was with my brother Muris at my uncle's, and we were there until 10.00 in the evening, and going back home, I noticed and heard the voice of Ivo Papic calling his son Dragan, "Dragan, come here, come here." And I even noticed a large number of personnel that had gathered there, but I didn't pay much attention because, quite frequently, people would gather in Dragan Papic's house. Sometimes there would be as many as 30 cars in the yard and the surroundings. So I assume it was some kind of a headquarters, a Storja, as they call it, so they would meet there quite often. It was not just our neighbours but people coming from further afield, like Vitez and Busovaca. So I didn't have any particular suspicions, I didn't pay much attention to these men who had gathered there, but Dragan Papic was certainly there the night before the attack, and his father.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Would you clarify his father as Ivo Papic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you know, by the way, where Drago Papic lived in that house, the house of his father Ivo. Did he live on the first floor or the second floor?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly. I don't remember that now. But in any event, one of them was on the top floor and the other one was on the ground floor, but I can't tell you exactly who was where.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, on the night of the 15th, you were returning home from your uncle's Sakib's house, you heard this conversation between father and son from across the road, Ivo and Dragan Papic, and you went home.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was a loud conversation, it was more like calls, they were calling each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And at that time, in your house, you lived with your brother, Muris, and who else, if you could tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I had a father, mother, and three sisters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're at the 3.30 mark and this may be a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. We will rise now. Thirty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Moskowitz, before you start, it just occurred to me that you didn't ask the witness to state his name and date of birth. Probably it would be appropriate at some stage to ask him about -- to identify the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Probably a good idea. Probably it would have been a better idea at the beginning, but it's a good idea now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Before we go on to the events of April 16, Mr. Ahmic, could you please state your full name and your date of birth for the record?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: My name is Abdulah Ahmic. I was born on the 29th of January, 1963.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you. And before we leave Exhibit 25, which is on that machine next to you, I want to state -- make it clear for the record, this is a blow-up of an area of Ahmici showing, at the top, the cemetery, and towards the bottom, the road that branches off from the main road into lower Ahmici and incorporates your immediate neighbourhood or the neighbourhood of Mr. Ahmic, and I want to also clarify, if we could, before we go on, Mr. Ahmic, and going back just briefly to the events in October '92, you indicated that your family and other families evacuated that part of Ahmici and that, over time, families returned. Your family returned, but could you tell us, was your family one of the first families to return or one of the last families to return in '92 to your home?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: It was one of the last families to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's move ahead to the morning of April 16, 1993, and to illustrate your testimony, I would ask the usher to show Exhibit, which I believe will be marked 26, to the witness. Mr. Ahmic, just to orient everyone and the Court and the Defence attorneys, could you point out where your house is on this Exhibit 26?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: It's here in the circle marked 38 (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you show the Court where the road into Ahmici off the main road is on this blow-up?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: So this is a blow-up of an area of Ahmici just below the first blow-up that we looked at, showing an area of your house now at the top of the map rather than at the bottom; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, tell us the first thing you remember happening on the morning of April 16, 1993, and feel free, when you so desire, to use the blow-up, Exhibit 26, to help you explain what happened.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: The first thing I remember was that I was awakened by a loud detonations (sic). This was in the early morning, dawn had not yet broken, and it went on for some 15 minutes, these terrible detonations. I presume it was an artillery attack against certain parts of our village. After that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, let me stop you before you continue on. You were in your house that morning, were you not?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was in my house. I was spending the night there. Me, my brother Muris, my father, and my three sisters, and we were all awakened by these detonations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What part of the house were you sleeping in and what part of the house were the other family members in at that time?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Muris was sleeping in the cellar and all the rest of us were sleeping on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: After the shelling, we didn't know what was going on. Then we looked out of the window -- I looked out of the window. The first thing I did was to call my brother Muris and ask him what we should do, and he said, "We can't go anywhere. The house is surrounded on all sides. We'll wait."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Before you go on -- I will occasionally interrupt you, I'm sorry. You had referred earlier to the fact that your brother Muris was one of the head of the TO in Ahmici back in 1992. Was he still a head of the TO in 1993 at the time of this attack?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No, he did not hold any post. He was supposed to go to work that morning. He had a job then. He was employed. He wasn't in the army at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Why was he no longer the head of the TO in '93?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: He was replaced or he resigned, I don't know exactly, but he was no longer ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Go ahead. Excuse me for interrupting, but proceed now with what you recall happening.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: The first thing I noticed was I noticed soldiers, five, six soldiers, here, near the house marked 35, the house of Ahmic Ida, and then near the house of Fahrudin Ahmic marked 37. This was almost simultaneous. There were four or five soldiers, they were carrying a canister and setting fire to this house, the house of Fahrudin Ahmic, number 37, and they were -- the soldiers were walking around this house so that we had no chance of going in this direction because this was the only direction in which we hoped we could get away, so that we were surrounded. Later, the soldiers, probably the woods were full of them here (indicating), near the house of Dragan and Pero Papic, later they came towards our house here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ahmic, you said you saw soldiers around the house of your next door neighbour Fahrudin --

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Again, that would be house number 37, Fahrudin's house?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, but these soldiers didn't come to our house, other soldiers came. I'll tell you later how this happened. After that, I heard a terrible detonation of a bomb and two bullets were fired. That was when my brother Muris was probably killed. Not much time had passed and then we heard shots, a round of shots shot at the front door of our house. There was no one in the corridor. My father and I went out. We opened the door. There were two soldiers. One was tall, blond, with a punk haircut with only a little hair in the middle of his head and they were painted in various colours. They had guns, they had bullet-proof suits, and one was -- the other one was about 170 centimetres tall with wavy, brown hair, and the tall one was about 190 centimetres tall and quite heavy in build. The first thing they asked us was whether we had any weapons. We said, "We don't have any weapons." I had a bomb, which I gave up to the tall one. And then the tall guy said to my father and me that we should go out into the yard, and he went into the house to search it. He returned quite soon and said to the younger man, "Do as ordered." This young man said, "I won't." Then he said to him again, "I order you to follow orders." And he said, "No, I won't." He told him that three times, and then he said, "I will execute the orders, but you will remember this." That's what he told him. And then he said, "Stay here and guard the women and the girls and I will carry out the orders." And then he ordered my father and me to pass around the southern side of the house. I'll tell you roughly, it was around this way (indicating), and we arrived here, and I noticed Muris's dead body facing the ground. He was wearing jeans. He had a light blue jacket and a black cap and Alpina, which is a brand of running shoes. And he said to my father, "Take two steps forward." My father was confused and unable to do so. Then he did, and he shot at him at point-blank range in the temple. I observed all this. Then he told me to take two steps forward. I obeyed, and he shot at me from one metre away, and the bullet entered here and went out here (indicating). I just felt warmth and I was spattered with blood. He turned away and I pretended to fall down or, rather, I fell down and remained lying there. Then I raised my head and looked round and saw no one nearby. And then, as fast as I could, I ran in this direction, there is a valley here, and I arrived at the road here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Ahmic, let me stop you there. When the soldiers entered your house, what were you wearing that morning?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I had quickly put on an old pair of jeans and an old pullover, something I could pull on quickly, so civilian clothes I used to wear around the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And what was your father wearing?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: He was also dressed, he had taken his blue Anorak which was hanging there and he put it on, and he was wearing trousers. He thought he was to be taken away somewhere to a camp or somewhere like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: When you were told to leave the house, what happened to the women in the house and the children in the house?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: They stayed behind. They remained in the house, in the corridor. They were pale. They were completely lost. They didn't know what was going on. They were completely lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: How many soldiers escorted you and your father out of the house?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: There were only two soldiers, and the ones at Fahrudin Ahmic's house were watching what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: How were these soldiers armed who escorted you out of the house?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: They were well-armed. They were well-armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell what kind of weapons they had?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: They had automatic rifles, I remember that. They didn't have those transport bags and the things carried by the army. They were people who did certain tasks. They were wearing bullet-proof suits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you or your father offer any resistance to these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No, no, none at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, when you and your father were escorted outside your home, at what point did you observe the body of your brother Muris and where was he lying?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Here. We noticed just around the corner, he was lying there about three metres away from the house. This is where we were both shot (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: How did your father react when he saw his son on the ground dead?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, it was very hard for him. Very hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, the soldier asked your father to step ahead, to step in front, before he shot him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, and he asked me to do the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Was your father able to comply with the soldier's orders to step ahead?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: It was hard. It was very hard for him to do that. Perhaps he couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And then you talked about some discussion between two soldiers about orders. Could you clarify, if you would, what you heard the two soldiers say to each other at this point?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: The tall one, when he came out of the house, he told the younger one, "Obey orders. Act as ordered." And he said "No." Then he said again, "Act as ordered." And he said "No." Then he told him for the third time, and he said "No." And then he threatened him and said, "Well, all right. I'll carry out the orders, but you'll remember this." That's how he said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What did you think they meant when they said, "Carry out the orders"? What orders do you think they were talking about?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I understood at once that they were going to kill us. That was a sign that they would kill us. There was an order by the commanders. It was obvious. Obviously, there was an order to kill.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you see your father when he was shot?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him. I saw the -- his brains coming out and blood spattering from his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And then what did the soldier say to you after they did that or he did that to your father?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Then he said to me, "Take two steps forward." I obeyed him. I took two steps forward, and then he aimed his gun and shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What were you thinking just before he shot?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: You can't think about anything. If any one of you here were to experience this, think about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Where were you shot? I think you tried to show us before. If you could point to where the bullet entered your head and where it exited?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Here, the bullet entered somewhere here, and this is where it came out, somewhere around here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you still have a mark where the bullet entered?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. If anyone wants, they can come up close and see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What happened after the bullet went through your head? What did you do next? What happened?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I realised that I was not dead, so I fell down, pretending to be dead, and I lay down on the ground and I remained lying still for a few moments. Then I slowly raised my head and I saw that there was no one nearby, so I started to run.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you, at this point, feel any pain or any discomfort?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No, there were no great pains. I was still bleeding, but the pain was not very bad, and, of course, a person must feel a terrible shock when he lives through something like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And so you lay on the ground for a little while, realised you weren't dead, looked around, and then moved to a different position. Could you show us on the blow-up beside you where you went?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: There is a valley here. I went this way and I went toward the north (indicating). I arrived at this road, the Vitez-Busovaca road, so I came out on the road hoping -- I forgot to say, while my father and I were being shot, there were UNPROFOR vehicles passing along this road. I hoped that a truck might come by and I could then be saved. I waited for five minutes, and then I noticed that nothing had come by, and I noticed that they were burning houses here (indicating), and soldiers were running in this direction, towards me. So there is a little bridge under the road here, and this is where I hid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, just to clarify your position at the time that you ran from your house after being shot. Where was the first position that you went to, and if you could refer on the blow-up to the markings so that we can see where you were, so that the record can be clear?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I think that I came to where this little line is (indicating). Then I went under the little bridge. It's about 10 metres away from this circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: There is a little line drawn right on the road next to the letter "V"?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There's a little bridge here, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: How did you hide under that bridge? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I was waist-deep in water. I hid there. I stayed there the whole day and half the night until 10.00 p.m., and I was in water all the time; and when soldiers passed by -- I'll tell you later in what direction they came -- I would submerge myself under the water so as not to be noticed, and I was wet the whole day until 10.00 p.m.; and then I noticed, just after I had hidden under the bridge, I noticed soldiers coming in the direction marked "2" and they distributed themselves in the direction of the arrows. There were 30 to 40 soldiers, it was the size of a platoon, and the first person who ran up was Ivica Safradin, he was a bald man, we used to call him Cica, he was the commander of the military police, and he was telling the soldiers to spread out in this direction. And I noticed Dragan Santic, Ilija Santic, Ilija Santic from Mahala, he had a moustache, he was married to a woman from Nadioci, he was in the military police as well; Tutic Blazo, who worked in Masinogradnja; Vlatko Kupreskic, who also worked there. I noticed some other people, Sureka Matkovic. There were about ten people I know. Some of them were wearing military uniforms as military policemen and some were dressed in civilian clothes. They were all armed and they were spreading out in this direction. Very soon, after they passed, another group came, again in the size of a platoon, 30 to 40 people, in completely black uniforms, such as were worn in World War II by the Ustasha, and they spread out a little further away from the first group. Then I noticed -- this was in the morning, about two or three hours later, during the day, soldiers began to arrive from the south, and they would come up to the point where I was and turn in this direction. These were groups of about ten soldiers, and they were exceptionally well-armed. They were wearing helmets and RP and RPG, these are anti-artillery or armed -- armed materials, and I forgot to say that they were wearing blue bands on their arms; and in the groups that arrived, some had green bands, some had black, white, yellow bands. Three to four groups of well-armed soldiers passed within a half-an-hour period in this direction. I also heard that a mortar had been brought to the vicinity, but I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned, Mr. Ahmic, that you saw military police. Did the military police have a specific kind of uniform that you could recognise?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had white belts and the insignia of the military police. This was easily noticeable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did these soldiers, all of these soldiers that you've described, did they appear to be acting in a coordinated way or were they acting -- were they fighting each other?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No. I think that they positioned themselves on the basis of a plan. The attack was probably directed towards this part of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And these were HVO soldiers then?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I noticed that some had HVO patches, others had HV patches, and even noticed a soldier close to me with the patch of Special Purpose Units, and I was able to read the words, and I was wondering what kind of units they were. I hadn't heard of them before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You refer to patches. What do you mean by "patches"?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the ribbons, the blue ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You said HVO patches, HOV patches, special purpose patches. What do you mean by patches? Where are they worn and what do they look like?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: These are worn here (indicating). They were this sort of shape, and you could see two rifles and something like that, and on top the letters HV or HVO, and the special purpose units I think had round patches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And do you know what "HVO" stood for?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: It stood for the Croatian Defence Council. It was the Croatian army in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and HV was the Croatian army. These were units of the Croatian army coming from Croatia, the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, these soldiers that you observed throughout the day, you observed them from under that bridge waist-deep in water; is that right? You have to answer.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: During the day, did you experience any more discomfort from your wound to your face?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was feeling dizzy, but I didn't faint.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you recall when about you finally got out of that ditch and out of that water that day?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I got out about 10.00 in the evening. I first went in this direction, but I came across a dugout. As far as I recall, I saw a small window on the dugout just near this letter "V." And there were three or four soldiers sitting on a fence and smoking. So I couldn't pass there. So I turned back and then I headed in this direction. However, these houses were burning and visibility was high, as if it was daytime. So after a short rest, there's a kind of a creek here, but here, where the Roman numeral VI is marked, there were again five or six soldiers smoking, and then I crawled along this creek for 50 or 60 metres and then I got into this house that is marked with the number 40. It was still smouldering, and I went in to dry. But as soon as I got in, I realised I had been discovered. There were eight soldiers positioned on all four sides of the building and there were two men walking along this way in completely white uniforms, rather like the European observers wore, but I didn't understand what they were doing there. I spent the night in that house. They didn't do anything. They didn't attack me. And in the morning, I noticed that six had left and two of them stood on guard, one on each side of the building. About 8.00, I heard the voice of my mother who was probably here, as Ivo Papic told me, she had spent the night with my sisters in Pero Papic's house, I heard her crying out and screaming, "They killed my husband and my sons," and they were probably taken somewhere. Ivo Papic told me later that he took them to a certain place. He took them to their death. He told me that he had taken them to the Bosniak lines, but, in fact, he left them somewhere there and they were killed by HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you mention that you heard your mother's voice in the house marked "H." That would be Pero Papic's house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And you were in house number 40 in the smouldering house?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And initially there were several soldiers around the house but that, in the morning, there were two soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What happened to you in that house later that day or in the morning?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: In the afternoon, nothing important happened except that around noon, I saw cars and tractors leaving Ahmici and going in the direction of Busovaca, some passenger cars and some tractors were driven away. What else did I notice that was important? It was about noon or about 1.00 in the afternoon. A car came and stopped here (indicating), military policemen got out, two of them, I don't remember whether there were more. They got out here, left the car, and went on foot up here, and soon after that, I saw thick smoke and a very strong blast, so they probably blew up the minaret of the mosque. They returned, they got into the car, and reached the spot where I was, right next to this house. I hear them getting out, and the person guarding me addressed him with the word "Commander," I saw that he was a military policeman, and he answered, "We have a Mujahedin here," and he said, "Throw a grenade in and kill him." And then he passed by here, I was sitting inside. He threw in a grenade, it fell right here. I just moved a little. It exploded, and I still cannot hear hardly at all on this ear. I pretended to be dead. And since they had brought a large quantity of explosives, dynamite, they continued to demolish things here. There was a plan here, Hasim Ahmic and a Croat had planned to set this factory up, but they blew it up, then a stable, then another yellow Yugo, a Yugo is the make of a car from Crvenie Zastava in Kragujevac, and then they left. They said good bye to these two, and then the one who threw in the grenade, he was middle-aged wearing a camouflage uniform with blond hair, he had a camouflage cap on his head, he was fair, and the other one was a child, he was 13 or 14, and he was also wearing a camouflage uniform and a cap, and both of them had rifles. They sat on the window and they watched me from a distance of a metre and a half or two, and they watched me for a long time. I lay there pretending to be dead. They must have noticed I wasn't dead. They watched me for quite a long time, I don't remember how long, and then the younger one said, "What are we waiting for? Why don't we throw in two more grenades and kill him?" And then this other one said, "No, let's go over here, there's dynamite. It will blow him up better." I started calling out. They were probably surprised. And then there were some building material here, some timber piled up, and they hid behind, and I stayed there waiting, didn't know what to do. Then I noticed Ivo Papic coming from his house and going along this way, he reached Simo Vidovic's house, which is somewhere around here, and shortly afterwards, they reached this part, Kasim Ahmic's stable, my uncle, I waved, and then they reached me, and they asked me who I was, what I wanted, and I introduced myself. I asked them to help me. I said they wanted to kill me. And they said, "Come out with us." And they took me out and they accompanied me to Zume along this road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Let's pause for a moment there, Mr. Ahmic, and just again to make the record clear, pertaining to the military policeman or police officers who you describe parking their vehicle at the junction of the main road and the road into Ahmici and who then went towards the lower mosque, could you again tell us that you saw those military police park at the circle in the blow-up marked Roman numeral VII; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is where they left their car. As far as I remember, they didn't use the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And you recognised them as military police because of the white belt which was distinctive for them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I even saw them here, right close up, when I peeked out, when they came up to me. They were some kind of commanders, but from the conversation, I realised they were from Busovaca because one of these men guarding me asked, "What's new in Busovaca?" And he said, "Everything is fine, it's under control." So I concluded that they had come from Busovaca, which is a town roughly the same size as Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And then to clarify, shortly after you saw the military police park their vehicle at Roman numeral VII, you heard a loud explosion from the direction of the lower mosque where they were heading when you lost sight of them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Very shortly afterwards. First, there was thick smoke as if tyres had been set on fire, and then a very strong explosion, and I saw the top of the minaret collapsing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ahmic, you indicated that you were taken out of that house that you referred to on the previous exhibit, Exhibit 26, I believe it was house 40, by Ivo Papic and could you then tell us where you were taken to and what route you took to get there?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I was taken along this road (indicating) and I noticed that all these houses marked with numbers were Bosniak houses, they were all destroyed and burnt, all the houses marked with numbers were Bosniak houses, and they took me in this direction, and I got to this house, somewhere here, the third house in the row. And there I found quite a large number of women and children who were put into rooms. They had been brought there before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, again to clarify the record, this exhibit, Exhibit 26, I believe, 27 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Twenty-seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Excuse me, thank you, 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Is a blow-up of the large Ahmici map that has already been introduced into evidence, and it shows the main road now farther down from where you were before and it focuses on what is known as the Santici area, and I believe earlier in your testimony you mentioned the area called Zume, and if you would, to orient everyone, where is Zume in this blow-up?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, my neighbours and me, we call this area Zume. They belong to the local community of Santici, but it was larger, and this smaller area was known as Zume. I don't think this was Zume. This, this is the area we referred to as Zume (indicating). But it all belonged to the local community of Santici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: It was a neighbourhood, if you will, maybe, of --

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, a hamlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: In-between perhaps Santici and Ahmici, would that be a way of describing it?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No, no. Zume belongs to Santici. It's part of Santici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: There are many houses here that you have circled. What do those circles indicate and what do they mean?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I marked the Bosniak houses that I saw had been destroyed when I passed along this road with Ivo and Simo. These are all Bosniak houses. It will take a long time for me to list all the names of the owners, but as you can see, there were many houses that were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And these were houses that you saw with your own eyes as you were walking down that main road to Santici?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, I notice there are other houses that don't have circles around them. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Those are houses belonging to Croats which were not damaged or destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you were taken by Ivo Papic, that would be the father of Dragan Papic, to the third house.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you then point out for us that third house, and I would, with the permission of the usher -- maybe you don't need the usher to help you -- there's a marker next to you. If you could draw a circle around that third house, if you would? It's a little bit of a fuzzy picture, so it may be difficult, but do your best. And could you also draw, while you have that marker with you, the direction of travel that you and Ivo Papic and the third gentleman took as you walked down from house 40 to that third house in Santici?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: (Marks).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, when you entered that third house in Santici, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I saw a large number of women and children. They were mostly women coming from these houses (indicating), those that had been burnt down and destroyed, but without their men, and others had been brought from the area where I used to live, women and children had been brought there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you describe the scene, the mood of the people that you saw in that third house, your former Muslim neighbours?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: All those women were in shock, they were petrified, mostly all of their men, husbands and sons had been killed. It was a most distressing situation, but also I wasn't in a position to really observe them because I was in the same situation as they.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What happened while you remained -- and by the way, this would be on April 17th, 1993, would it not?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What happened while you were in this third house in Santici?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: They gave us a little food, they brought some food from the neighbouring houses, and then during the night, about 10.00, three soldiers came in, and they said they needed a man to go to the UNPROFOR base. Apparently -- allegedly to ask for lorries to take us to Zenica. And then he addressed me and said, "Why don't you go?" And I refused. I said I couldn't, that I was feeling faint, and I would probably have been killed if they had taken me out because it was night time. During the night, nothing important happened. I remember that nearby, at this junction, there was an anti-aircraft canon firing in the direction of the Mahala. That's all that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You mention Mahala. Would you describe what that is?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: It is a Catholic village north-west of my village or north of Santici. It is on an elevation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, did you speak to anyone or did anyone speak to you when that soldier came into the third house and was looking for a man to go to UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. (redacted) whispered in my ear, don't go. That is how they took out three men, allegedly to bury the dead, but they never returned, which means they killed those men, and this is why she whispered this to me. And maybe I would have gone to ask for those lorries, but I changed my mind, and anyway, I really was feeling faint and I doubt I could have got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And (redacted), former neighbour of yours, who lived in the Zume area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: How did it come about that you were able to leave that third house in Santici, you and the other people?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: We spent the night there, and at about 8.00 in the morning, Nicika Plavcic came, he was an artist from Vitez, and he told me that we would be exchanged, that all of us were going to be exchanged, and that the exchange would take place in Tolovici, if I remember well, at the line of confrontation. Apparently there were captured Croats in Poculica, and we would be exchanged. What he did, in fact, was he took us to the Dubravica school to a camp. As soon as we entered the school playground, the soldiers shut us up. Also, there were trenches around the school, so this was a real military camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, this Dubravica school that you were taken to, how did you and the other people who were being held captive in the third house, how did you get from that house in Santici to the Dubravica school?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: We all went on foot along the road. It was about three or four kilometres away along an asphalt road in the direction of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: This Dubravica school, am I right in saying that it is located near the conjunction of the mountain road to Zenica and the main Busovaca-Vitez road that you've described?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: It is a regional road, not a mountain road. Yes, it is close to that road, and it is close to the main Vitez-Busovaca road, very close, only it's on a slope.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: So you and the other displaced persons, mostly women and children, walked or had to walk to the Dubravica school; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Describe the conditions at the Dubravica school, if you would.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: When we got there, there were about 30 or 40 men there already, mostly from Vitez, Gacice, who had been brought there, as they told us, two hours before us. They had also been captured. At the entrance to the school, they separated the younger women and the children in one set of classrooms, whereas they took us into the gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: When you say "us," you mean the men?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No, the older women and those who were weak, the infirm, but there were some younger women in the gym too, but still they did separate some people and put them up in the classrooms. There were women even in the gym with children. I don't know why they were separating them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: How many days did you spend at the Dubravica school, you and the others?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I spent five or six days there. The others stayed longer. Having been wounded, I left earlier because the Red Cross came and some doctors, and they took me to Zenica. Others, I think, stayed for a month and some even longer in that school. I think that only five or six of us left under Red Cross escort to Zenica on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What was the condition of your wound at the time you left Dubravica school?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: My face had swollen up and I was in bad shape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: While at the Dubravica school, if you could give us just a brief idea of the conditions there and of incidents that may have occurred while you were there that you recall?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: At first, the food was very poor. They gave us very little. Later on, they allowed Bosniak women, who were not captured from the surrounding houses, to bring us food. The conditions were such that we were lying on the floor. There were no blankets or anything. Later on, they brought some. Then the first night, they took men to dig trenches to the surrounding villages to reinforce the lines. The unit leaders would come. I remember Ivica Safradin coming, looking for men to go to Pirici, I think it was. And then Vlatko from Krcevine came, "Cicin" he was called. He's my age. He was looking for men for Krcevine. He was the worst. He really mistreated those men who he took with him. These unit leaders would come several times a day and even during the night to take men out. Some men would come back wounded, exhausted, mistreated, so that the conditions were very bad. There were even cases that a man was killed, and they would come back with wounds sometimes. Who wounded them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: How were the women treated?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that I noticed that there were instances of rape, especially where the younger women were in the classrooms. Next to me, a young man lay, and his wife had been separated from him. One morning his wife visited him crying, so I concluded that she had been raped. And the rumour was that there were rapes in this camp, in this school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Before we leave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Moskowitz, I'm sorry to interrupt you. How much time do you need, because it's 5.00. It occurs to me that we should stop now, if you can tell us --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I have actually just one more question on this exhibit, and then I think we ought to break -- I would think that would be a good idea -- and probably another -- I just want to show him some photographs, and that can take sometimes a little time, and that would essentially conclude the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Your estimate was of an hour and a half. Anyway ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You can put one more question and then we'll break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, looking at Exhibit 27, I believe, on the machine next to you, you had testified earlier that you had seen Dragan Papic back in '92/'93 with a sniper rifle and a strangling device, and you had mentioned it was somewhere down in Zume and Santici. We didn't have on the ELMO at that time that area of the map. We do now. Could you show us where you saw Dragan Papic between '92 and '93 carrying those weapons?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I saw him here (indicating) at this junction leading to Rovna. I was coming in this way, and he and his brother Goran were going the opposite way, and we met here (indicating). Maybe we just exchanged greetings briefly. This is where we met, at this cross-roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. We will rise now. I'm sorry, one second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, may I make a remark? The witness has stated that Vlatko Kupreskic knows Blazo Tutic because they worked together in Masinogradnja, a company called Masinogradnja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. In cross-examination, you can ask any question. Why do you want to put this question now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: No, this has to do with a correction of the transcript, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: It seems to us that the transcript was not correct regarding this particular part of the witness's statement, and one may be able to conclude from this that the witness actually saw Vlatko Kupreskic. I'm sure that somebody will check this, but I would like to draw your attention to this. Either we should correct the transcript or the witness should be asked once again to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. Thank you. We will ask the registrar to check the transcript. In any case, if there is any doubt, this question will be put again tomorrow so as to clarify the position of the witness. Thank you. We will rise now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 5.06 p.m. to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 19th day of August, 1998 at 9.30 a.m. 25
